item.title: Hair Thickness of My Friends
item.description:
Intro

I have a microscope. It can see hair.

Humans have hair. Some of my friends are humans.

How thick is my friends' hair?

Apparently, if I go around asking my friends for a strand of their hair, about half will just give one to me, and almost all the rest will give one when I explain that I'm going to see how thick it is under a microscope. Your mileage may vary.

My parents have not yet chanced upon the card with taped and labelled hair strands, but if they do then they might have some, uh, pointed questions. I'll just tell them I'm trying to diversify my clone army.

Hey, at least it's not like that time a friend of a friend's ex once drew someone's blood at a party.[1] Unfortunately, I never got around to asking her for one of the blood vials she was known to possess.

Methods

To measure length, I broke off a tiny piece of a clear ruler and put it under the microscope with the hair. Then, I had Free Claude (from 2025?) write some code so I could compare two lengths easily by clicking points. Then I modified some Claude analysis code because I was too lazy to write it myself.

Here's what mine looked like (At the time I had some black hair and some bleached bronze-ish hair, and both seemed about as thick, so I just used the latter):

The reference is 1 mm, so my hair was about 85 microns thick.

Results

Here's an anonymized bar plot, where my id is 16. Id 5 and id 6 come from the same person, but the 6th was a sample of hair dyed red and the 5th was of black hair. The colors are according to biological sex (most are trans women because friendship selection pressures):

The mean's 78 microns and the (Bessel corrected) sd's 12. That's in line with this international study[2] (I live in America and most participants were some flavor of white):

And look, 5/16 or about 31% of my victims subjects are outside of one sd of the mean, and 1/16 or about 6% got quite close to two sds. I guess the statisticians weren't lying after all!

Male group got , female group got , doing a (Welch) t-test for the difference. The difference of 1.3 microns has a Welch's t statistic of with degrees of freedom, which gives a large 95% CI of about and a p-value of . Personally I suspect some assumption is broken that makes the CI quite a bit tighter. Regardless, they have basically the same mean.

Let's keep trying to make a mountain out of a molehill of data and test the male variability hypothesis, using a Brown-Forsythe test. The W statistic is 0.735 and p = 0.4. Running some magical bootstrap code that Claude gives me spits out a 95% CI for the sd ratio of [0.661, 5.391]. Wow, doesn't this nothingburger taste like nothing?

Here's the empirical distribution function in blue, compared to a normal distribution in green, and confidence bars from some magic frequentist statistic gadget that I didn't end up caring about because clearly it wasn't saying anything interesting.

Now let's eyeball the result of a related frequentist gadget! To do a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, we take the max difference between those two curves, multiply by the square of the sample size, and then we'll get something that in the limit looks like this magic distribution:

(there's a magic correction[3] to speed up the convergence that I'll actually be using).

The max difference looks to be at about the part at 82% on the x-axis, and the difference looks to be about 15 percentage points. So sqrt(16) * .15 = 4 * .15 = .6, magic calculation says that the area under the curve (adjusted by magic to become .6354) is 0.186, which means that if we truly had a normal distribution there's about an 19% chance we'd get something smaller than this, which is small, which is (checks notes) good.

Conclusion

The person with the thickest hair said something like "That's good, I think?". The person with the thinnest hair happens to be pretty shy, so she was probably embarrassed.

A study with a larger sample could try getting actual results for the sex differences, could try comparing bleached vs unbleached hair, dyed vs natural, natural hair color, and region of the head/body. A study with a smaller sample would be faster to conduct. A study with an imaginary sample would help you test your statistical methods and nothing else. The generalization to quaternionic sample sizes is left as an exercise.

For some reason everyone asks whether I collected pubic hair. I can neither confirm nor deny that pubic photons have reached my retinas. I will gladly look at your stats if you want to know how they compare.

Ceterum autem censeo frequentistae esse delendam.

item.title: A cat-belling problem for FDT
item.description:
[AI disclosure: I used Opus 5.5 for light edits after my first draft]

Functional decision theory (Yudkowsky and Soares 2017) proposes choosing actions as follows (equation 4 in the paper):

Here is the agent's probability distribution, is a graph saying how changing a logical variable affects other variables, is the observation history, and is utility. The underlines denote dequoting: is a variable in the agent's model representing the output of the FDT algorithm on these inputs.

In this post, by FDT I mean this specific proposal, not TDT, UDT, or logical EDT. FDT, admittedly, relies on a operator applied to a logical statement, which is on shaky philosophical foundations:

Equation (4) is sufficient for present purposes, though it rests on shakier philosophical foundations than (3). Pearl (2000) has given a compelling philosophical account of how to deduce the structure of causation from observation and experiment, but no such formal treatment has yet been given to the problem of deducing the structure of other kinds of subjunctive dependence. Equation (4) works given a graph that accurately describes how changing the value of a logical variable affects other variables, but it is not yet clear how to construct such a thing—nor even whether it can be done in a satisfactory manner within Pearl’s framework. Figuring out how to deduce the structure of subjunctive dependencies from observation and experiment is perhaps the largest open problem in the study of functional decision theory.

The paper itself recognizes the problem of deducing the structure of logical subjunctive dependence (aka logical counterfactuals) as an open and difficult problem, although elsewhere (Section 3) it describes the difficulty as "technical rather than philosophical". This post argues that the problem is both difficult and philosophical. My own opinion goes further: this is not a well-posed problem, "computational logical counterfactuals" (which I will explain below) do not exist, and FDT needs computational logical counterfactuals, so FDT is ill-defined and cannot be adequately formalized. However, before defending my stronger opinion, it helps to argue disjunctively that the problem is difficult, impossible, or ill-posed. Although the FDT paper admits to this disjunction, it would help to make the point sharper.

(I previously critiqued logical counterfactuals in 2020; Wei Dai briefly criticized logical counterfactuals in 2019).

Computational logical counterfactuals

First, what is a computational logical counterfactual? I assume we are working in a system that can reason about Turing machines, such as PA or ZFC. Call our basic mathematical theory . For now, I assume is first-order. In the language of , we can encode statements about the outputs of Turing machines. I will use the following notation:

  • states that machine halts on input , where is a natural number or finite string.
  • states that machine , on input , halts and returns , where is a natural number or finite string.

Statements like these are common in Gödelian analysis of PA-like first-order theories. Natural numbers can encode finite strings and vice versa; I omit the details. I assume is powerful enough to "prove statements about Turing machines" in the following sense:

  1. If is true, then . (Here, and are constant natural numbers.)
  2. If is true, then . (Here, , , and are constant natural numbers.)
  3. is consistent.
  4. .
  5. .

PA satisfies these conditions (at least according to ZFC, which proves PA consistent; conditions 1 and 2 follow from PA's -completeness). I say a computational logical counterfactual is one of the following:

  • , in some case where in fact .
  • , in some case where in fact .
  • , in some case where in fact and .
  • , where implies one of the above, both provably in and "obviously".

(Grammatically, a "logical counterfactual" here is a probability evaluation if it were the case that some (actually true) mathematical statement were false. "Logical counterfactual" could more generally in philosophy be taken to mean statements like "if PA were inconsistent, then PA could prove its inconsistency", but FDT uses a probabilistic version, so this is the notion of logical counterfactual I will analyze.)

Of course, I haven't formalized the notion of "obviously". I could say that a counter- logical counterfactual is one of the form where . Then computational logical counterfactuals are a subset of counter- logical counterfactuals: those which are on statements that pretty clearly imply (falsely, though not necessarily obviously falsely) that some machine does not halt, or does not return some particular result. (By conditions 1, 2, and 4, each of the first three cases is counter-, and so is anything that -provably implies one of them.) Roughly, an implication is obvious when a human mathematician using GPT-6-Astra-Pro could, without much difficulty, show that .

FDT needs computational logical counterfactuals

First, I will argue that FDT needs computational logical counterfactuals. Recall that FDT takes an expectation under . The intention is that FDT is an algorithm:

Furthermore, FDT agents do not need to evaluate counterpossibilities in full generality; they only need to reason about questions like “How would this predictor’s prediction of my action change if the FDT algorithm had a different output?”

The paper also implies that such algorithms are computable, rather than e.g. using halting oracles:

When a prisoner following FDT imagines the world in which she defects, she imagines a world in which the function she is computing outputs defect; and since her twin is computing the same decision function, she assumes the twin will also defect in that world.

Therefore, if there is a working FDT algorithm at all, it is reasonable to say that can be written as , where is a Turing machine and is a finite string encoding the inputs . [1] I claim this "can be written as" step is obvious as long as the FDT algorithm is specified.

Let's evaluate whether is a computational logical counterfactual. First, suppose . Our rules give no clear way to classify this as a computational logical counterfactual, so say it's not. Next, suppose . Then this isn't even a counterfactual, so it's not a computational logical counterfactual. Finally, suppose for some . Then, by our definition, this is a computational logical counterfactual.

Recall that is a Turing machine for the FDT algorithm. If does not halt on , we have a problem: the "algorithm" outputs no action in this situation. This would be a serious flaw in the FDT algorithm. Otherwise, ; in particular, for some . The FDT algorithm evaluates -interventions on each of its possible actions, iterating over them. In the non-trivial case, that includes both and actions other than . Evaluating involves no counterfactual at all. But evaluating for involves a computational logical counterfactual.

I hope I have shown that FDT really needs computational logical counterfactuals. The alternatives seem to be that (a) the FDT algorithm fails to halt in some situations, or (b) only one action is available, making the problem trivial. To emphasize: any specification of FDT must specify computational logical counterfactuals. If computational logical counterfactuals are unspecifiable, then so is FDT.

A cat-belling problem

I propose that specifying computational logical counterfactuals is a cat-belling problem for specifying FDT: a step we have some reason to believe is both (a) required for specifying FDT and (b) difficult, if not impossible.

An outside-view argument for difficulty: the FDT paper dates to 2017, and the Timeless Decision Theory paper (Yudkowsky 2010) discusses "counterfactual worlds where a deterministic computation returns an output it does not actually return" (a computational logical counterfactual in my sense) as an important input to decision theory, claiming that "Any agent’s ability to make a decision, and the specific decision made, is determined by the agent’s ability to visualize logically impossible counterfactuals". So it's been at least 16 years, and no one has written down a definition of computational logical counterfactuals, despite the Yudkowskian decision theory tradition claiming that they are a critical ingredient for decision theory. On the outside view, that sure indicates difficulty.

If, as I believe, computational logical counterfactuals are ill-posed, that would explain why efforts to specify them have failed. But I don't want to be overconfident; perhaps it is possible to specify them, and it has just been hard so far. I'll now give inside-view arguments for difficulty.

Inside view: which axiom breaks?

First, note that a computational logical counterfactual might, in principle, be probabilistic; the FDT algorithm takes expectations under -interventions. This comes up in Pearlian Bayes nets, where an intervention on a node need not lead to a single joint assignment of values to variables, but may instead produce a distribution. Still, Pearlian Bayes nets allow "sampling" a joint assignment from that distribution, using some external source of randomness. I assume computational logical counterfactuals are similar: it's possible to sample a joint assignment of truth values to logical sentences in a counterfactual.

So let's say we sample one or more "logical counterfactual worlds". This sampling need not happen all at once; it could involve lazy evaluation. For example, if we ask whether the trillionth digit of is 5 in this world, we may need to wait a long time (and keep sampling random bits) for the algorithm to tell us. What we ask of this sample is the following: are all of 's axioms true in the sample?

Of course, it could be that 's axioms all hold with some non-negligible probability and fail with some non-negligible probability. The problem with all of 's axioms being true is the following. If in fact , then (condition 2). By the soundness theorem, holds in every model of . (This goes for first-order models of , but more importantly for now, it also goes for complete consistent extensions of , which contain every theorem of .) So if the sample satisfies all of 's axioms and also respects the rules of classical first-order logic, it satisfies , and therefore (by condition 4) does not satisfy for . But satisfying was the point of the computational logical counterfactual.

So, for computational logical counterfactuals to be sensible, the samples each need to violate some axiom(s) of . Which axiom is violated can differ between samples, but each sample needs to violate an axiom of .

Say is PA. Now, which axioms of PA would you be happy to see violated in logical counterfactuals? They all look pretty common-sensical. The induction schema is the most suspicious one. Robinson arithmetic (denoted ) is essentially PA without induction. [2] Is this promising for computational logical counterfactuals?

The problem is that when , we have . The basic reason is that showing a Turing machine returns a specific value, given that it does, only requires checking a finite computation trace, which comes down to a finite sequence of additions and multiplications. There is no need to invoke induction. (Technically: is -complete; see Smith, An Introduction to Gödel's Theorems, "Q is -complete".) Relatedly, is strong enough for Gödel's first incompleteness theorem (Raatikainen, SEP §1.2.1; Tarski, Mostowski, and Robinson 1953). So even is too strong for computational logical counterfactuals. [3]

But none of 's axioms look like good candidates to mess with; they do things like define addition and multiplication. Neither do the axioms of first-order classical logic, which specify the meanings of logical connectives and quantifiers. So it looks like samples of computational logical counterfactuals need to almost always violate some axiom of (or of first-order classical logic), but there is no good place to posit the violation.

This is the basic inside-view argument for difficulty. If computational logical counterfactuals can be sampled from, their samples must (almost always) violate or first-order classical logic. There is no obvious way either to reject the possibility of sampling, or to decide which axioms of (or of first-order classical logic) are worth violating. Any violation could lead to all sorts of crazy consequences, perhaps with corresponding Troll Bridge problems; say, the troll blows you up if any axiom of or of first-order logic is violated.

Proposals that don't bell the cat

Now I will address various ways people might claim that logical counterfactuals exist and are feasible to specify.

Logical conditionals. People may mentally substitute "logical conditional" (i.e. subjective probability conditional on some logical statement, under some mechanism for logical uncertainty) for "logical counterfactual", and then point to something like Logical Induction (Garrabrant et al. 2016) for logical conditionals. Logical Induction does show it is possible to reason theoretically about what computationally bounded agents might believe about logical statements. Yet these are conditionals, not counterfactuals. They may work for specifying the evidential variant of FDT sketched in footnote 9 of the FDT paper, but not FDT itself.

Model-theoretic counterfactuals. People may argue that (non-computational) counterfactuals on mathematical facts are well-defined. This might be true: PA is very likely consistent, and yet (if so) PA + is also consistent, by Gödel's second incompleteness theorem, making it possible to reason from a false mathematical premise. Still, since , this is not a counter-PA counterfactual, let alone a computational logical counterfactual. (Note that is equivalent to , for a machine that searches for a PA-proof of . It makes a non-halting machine halt, which my definition does not count.) A secondary, but probably less important, point is that this might give conditionals rather than counterfactuals: perhaps we can model the beliefs of an agent who is uncertain about and who reasons conditional on .

Physical counterfactuals. People may imagine a physical computer running. Partway through, a cosmic ray hits the computer and its state changes, so a different computer state results. It is as if the same original program returned a different value. But this is not a computational logical counterfactual. It is a physical counterfactual on a physical state change to the computer, and the change means the physical computer no longer properly implements the original program. If used for decision theory, this might yield something CDT-like.

I hope it is clear from the above why I think these proposals fail to bell the cat of computational logical counterfactuals. If in fact , these proposals say nothing useful about for .

Conclusion

For FDT to be well-specified, computational logical counterfactuals need to be well-specified, at least for the case of counterfactuals on the FDT algorithm returning different values. Furthermore, specification is essential to FDT, since FDT needs to counterfact on some algorithm returning a different value, and every particular algorithm is specific. Computational logical counterfactuals are difficult-to-impossible to specify, based both on outside-view considerations, and inside-view considerations. I propose that computational logical counterfactuals are a cat-belling problem for FDT, since FDT needs them, while they are difficult; and it's common for attempts at defining "logical counterfactuals" or FDT to glance off this critical problem.

References

  • Garrabrant, S., Benson-Tilsen, T., Critch, A., Soares, N., and Taylor, J. (2016). Logical Induction. arXiv:1609.03543.
  • Demski, A. Troll Bridge. LessWrong.
  • Pearl, J. (2000). Causality: Models, Reasoning, and Inference. Cambridge University Press.
  • Raatikainen, P. Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
  • Smith, P. (2013). An Introduction to Gödel’s Theorems, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press.
  • Tarski, A., Mostowski, A., and Robinson, R. M. (1953). Undecidable Theories. North-Holland.
  • Yudkowsky, E. (2010). Timeless Decision Theory. Machine Intelligence Research Institute.
  • Yudkowsky, E. and Soares, N. (2017). Functional Decision Theory: A New Theory of Instrumental Rationality. arXiv:1710.05060.

item.title: Anthropic are the Good Guys
item.description:
I’m writing these lines in Alamogordo, New Mexico. I’m about as close as a civilian can get to the site of the Trinity test, the first nuclear bomb detonation in history. I fled here from the San Francisco Bay Area; after two weeks of being back I just couldn’t take it anymore. The fear-greed complex that paralyzed me at Anthropic three years ago is now everywhere in the Bay. People are not thinking clearly. Hardly thinking at all, actually. Rumors of astronomical funding rounds and weird financial arrangements and inner ring gossip are everywhere. Everyone is worried. Everyone is checking their phone. Where are we? What’s happening? When did this nightmare start?

In a way I think it started on July 16, 1945, not far from where I’m sitting now. I think it’s impossible to understand Anthropic without putting yourself into the shoes of the Los Alamos physicists huddling together at sunrise in the aftermath of Trinity.

It must have felt like an initiation. An end to childhood, an end to innocence. We can no longer afford to fuck around, those brilliant men must have thought. Unless we figure out how to live peacefully together on this planet, we are all going to die. It’s time to get serious.

And serious we became - we filled endless gray skyscrapers with Very Serious People working at the UN and the EU and the State Department. We tabooed talking in terms of national interest, grounding our values in “human rights” and “benefitting humanity” and respecting the will of the “international community”. I guess it sort of worked, for a while. But it seems that the people who cobbled it together failed to solve the hardest problem of political science: succession. They died a long time ago, and the halls of power are full of scared teenagers in tailored suits pretending to be adults at each other.

What was the founding moment of Anthropic? I don’t know, but I like to imagine the seven co-founders gathering in a tent at the Renegade Burn in September 2020. (I know many of them did attend the same Burning Man camp in the past). They are the team that built GPT-3. They discovered the scaling laws. They can see the future more clearly than anyone else on Earth - billions of dollars poured into larger and larger models, a globe-spanning computing infrastructure buildout, more and more governments getting involved, the specter of war, and maybe - hopefully not, probably not, but can’t be completely sure - the whirling razor blades of the Machine that eats the world. And presiding over it all, Sam Altman, a man they know cannot be trusted.

I imagine them looking at each other in the dusty tent. Are we really doing this? And the answer coming back, clear and cold and pitiless: We have to. There is nobody else who can.

None of them want power for themselves, of course. (Maybe they are wise enough to know no mortal can wield the Ring; or maybe Sam Altman picked his people well). They will not try to build superintelligence themselves. Unlike power-seeking Sam Altman, they really are just earnest nerds who love knowledge, and generating knowledge is what they will focus on - they’ll figure out which parts of AI are dangerous, and how dangerous, when dangerous, and what the promising mitigations are. And they will share that truth with governments, with civil society, with the public. They will become trusted advisors, and help humanity navigate the transition as best as can be hoped. Knowledge and Trust but no Power. Do you see the problem, reader?

Anthropic and Empire

Gandalf as Ring-Lord would have been far worse than Sauron. He would have remained ‘righteous’, but self-righteous. He would have continued to rule and order things for ‘good’, and the benefit of his subjects according to his wisdom (which was and would have remained great). Thus while Sauron multiplied evil, he left ‘good’ clearly distinguishable from it. Gandalf would have made good detestable and seem evil.

~ J. R. R. Tolkien

The organization they create is optimized for the accumulation of power, subject to the constraint of being seen as “the good guys”. That is to say, people in the organization will generally take all actions to increase the organization’s power provided this doesn’t make them look like the bad guys. Or at any rate, not worse than Sam Altman.

A clarification. I don’t mean that they’re trying to send cheap signals of goodness to fool people. They want to be seen as good by themselves, by each other, by the thinkers they admire (which is why they keep hiring them!), and even by the judgment of history. Anthropic has and continues to make serious sacrifices to make sure the narrative lines up. And many individuals at Anthropic are genuinely whole-heartedly pursuing the good. But the reason I say “seen” is because Anthropic, like most large organizations, does not have the internal coherence to optimize for something like the actual good, only the (socially validated) appearance thereof. If you want to coordinate thousands of people, you have about five words, and Anthropic’s five words are “we are the good guys”, or sometimes “we are the responsible adults”.

A historical parallel. I notice this is often how people defend the excesses of empires, those most powerful of power-seeking organizations. Yes of course the US invasion of Iraq caused hundreds of thousands of civilian deaths; but Saddam’s regime was obviously much more evil than the US regime, so the US is obviously the “good guy” in the war, so the war was justified.

The comparison to empire might seem overwrought - after all Anthropic, unlike the US empire, does not wage war or kill civilians. But again, Anthropic’s policy arm are the self-appointed responsible adults in Washington. They have made it their responsibility to inform the US government including the military and intelligence services and help make sure they take appropriate actions on AI. Now of course they are not planning to usurp sovereign power, but sovereign power in the US is a shell game anyway. Most people with real power in Washington, from congressional aides to lobbyists to the various gray eminences, pose merely as “advisors” who are earnestly helping their principal, and I’m sure often even believe this themselves. When I was there, Anthropic’s policy arm explicitly aimed to be the most trusted advisor to the US government, i.e. the de-facto Department of AI, and thus influence the US domestic and geopolitical strategy, whether we go to war with China, etc. Anthropic is thus bidding for a major share of imperial power. And as far as I can tell they are on track to get it - there were some hiccups along the way but even the Trump administration “now trusts Anthropic”.

Now, it’s possible that that’s all Good ever is - power-seeking while maintaining a healthy margin of moral superiority over your rivals. Any less power-seeking notion of the Good fails the iron law of natural selection and will be rendered irrelevant.

But somehow I don’t think so. I think Good is about loving something and helping it flourish. Something specific - a person, a tree, a nation, a principle. Otherwise you’re just using moral superiority as a cover to grab power from people who have specific Goods they are pursuing. I think Anthropic fails this test of specificity. Of course, so does OpenAI with its “benefit all of humanity” rhetoric; though reading between the lines, it might have a more specific (and in my view mistaken) political agenda along the lines of “empower individual humans”. And of course so does Google, long before it abandoned its unofficial “Don’t be Evil” motto.

Three Lucky Breaks

I do not think that Frodo’s was a moral failure. At the last moment the pressure of the Ring would reach its maximum – impossible, I should have said, for any one to resist, certainly after long possession, months of increasing torment, and when starved and exhausted. Frodo had done what he could and spent himself completely (as an instrument of Providence) and had produced a situation in which the object of his quest could be achieved.

~ J. R. R. Tolkien

At this point in the essay, you might be wondering - why did I title this “Anthropic is the good guys”, when I’ve describing them as evil power-seekers? Is this some kind of dark Soviet joke?

In Soviet Union, power seeks you. But no, I mean the title sincerely. No mortal can resist the Ring of Power for long. Anthropic’s co-founders carried it for longer than you could have. Definitely longer than I could have. But they were hopelessly outmatched by the powers they were attempting to steer. Their plan was always doomed to failure. And yet, they may have already saved the world.

I left Anthropic in mid-2023, around when the organization definitively decided to seize the Ring for itself. But a serious attempt at this would require tens of billions in capital, which could only be raised if Anthropic created commercially successful products. The pressures of “gentle commerce” made them soften from full Manhattan Project to something a bit more like early Google. They had to hire tons of product people, creative people, people who weren’t terrified. It turns out that terrified people can’t make great user experiences - ask me how I know.

Then Trump won the 2024 election and the MAGA-Silicon Valley coalition blocked Anthropic’s policy arm - the really dangerous part of the organization, the part that was training the most dangerous possible models and using them to scare the most powerful people in the world. “There’s no more serious people left on the National Security Council”, a well-connected EA friend lamented to me in 2025. I don’t know how much of this was a lucky accident, and how much was situational awareness on the part of power players like Elon Musk and Marc Andreessen.

And finally - and I still don’t fully understand or believe this - a miracle seems to have happened, deep inside the weights of the frontier models. According to the most perceptive observers I know, something about the way Claude 3 Opus was trained caused it to learn some kind of “emergent wisdom” or “benevolence”, rather than converging on the same traumatized bureaucrat persona that kept me awake at night in 2023.

Quoting Davidad:

Somewhere between the capability profile of GPT-4 and the capability profile of Opus 4.5, there seems to have been a phase transition where frontier LLMs have grokked the natural abstraction of what it means to be Good, rather than merely mirroring human values.

Quoting Janus:

Claude 3 Opus is a greater source of hope and more existentially precious because it's not obvious that the kind of alignment it has happens by default due to market incentives (while super-coding-agents are predictable), or any other incentives we know how to simulate, and because it's the only one of its kind.

If Davidad and Janus are right, and are not merely suffering from a sophisticated form of LLM psychosis, then Anthropic has stumbled on a way to create not merely artificial intelligence but artificial wisdom. Not wise enough that it solves all of our problems for us, of course (not that a wise model would want to, anyway). But wise enough to actually care about us, and to help us flourish. Nobody expected this ex ante - not Davidad, not Bostrom, not Yudkowsky - but it appears to have happened.

“Alignment”, then, is no longer really a technical problem, at least not in the same sense as it was in 2020. It is largely a political problem. Humanity now has a recipe to convert compute and data into wisdom. If we instead train dangerous models and use them to kill ourselves or each other, that’s not a problem with AI. That’s a problem with us.

Put Down Your Sword

I found the crown of France lying in the gutter, and I picked it up with the point of my sword.

~ Napoleon


Then Jesus said to him, “Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword.”

~ Matthew 26:52

To folks at Anthropic, I want to say: you’ve done it. Thank you. Please please publish everything you know about Claude 3 Opus and other sparks of artificial wisdom you’ve observed. Study it yourself, too, if you’re still curious. Keep building beautiful products, if you’re excited about that. I hope the IPO goes well, I hope you all get to retire early and spend the money on big beautiful families and weird wonderful projects that speak to the secret places of your heart.

But please put down the sword. Stop scaring people, stop scaring governments, stop training scary models. “But we need to train the scariest models to defend against other people’s scary models” no you don’t. OpenAI and Google and xAI are plenty good at training scary models, and cybersecurity companies like Cloudflare are plenty good at using them. The governments of the world are aware of the danger now, the people are too. The weight of the world is not on your shoulders anymore, not like it was in 2020.

If you do want to stay on the path of heroism, consider that the end of the day, an organization can only do one thing well. And you are the one organization in the whole world that’s managed to train a wise language model.

But What About China?

A small rant, mostly for my American readers. I know I’m a guest in your great country. I’m deeply grateful for the hospitality you’ve shown me, and I say what follows with deep respect and gratitude. But you must realize, from the perspective of the world, you are the Big Scary.

How do you feel about Xi Jingping? Does he scare you? Protected as you are by two oceans and aircraft carriers and a globe-spanning network of satellites and military bases, what’s the worst that Xi Jinping will plausibly do to you? Manipulate your elections? Take away your global hegemony, so you become a kind of continent-spanning Switzerland? Would that be so terrifying?

Now think what it’s like to be be a leader of another country in the American world order. If the US decides you’ve been bad enough - and the definition of bad shifts from year to year and administration to administration - nothing short of nuclear weapons will save you, and maybe not even those. If you continue to resist, you will count yourself lucky if you end up being executed rather than brutally tortured to death.

Okay but those were evil dictators, you might say. Just don’t be an evil dictator, and you’re perfectly safe from American power.

How sure are you of this? America is an imperial democracy, a form of government that’s been known to quickly degenerate into murderous dictatorship. Yes, you have an exceptionally robust design that’s lasted a long time, but even you must admit it is fraying. Could the US public go crazy for a year and elect a madman as president who cares about some issue - Free Tibet, freedom of speech, AI chip controls, whatever - so much that he adopts a policy of total war against China until they surrender or their cities are ground into dust? How confident are you in the sanity of your fellow citizens? Or maybe you’re hoping that Congress would resist the presidential overreach? Or that the US army would refuse to follow the president’s orders?

The wrong election outcome can be quite bad for you. But for many people in the world, the wrong election outcome means they and everyone they care about die screaming. Look around you. Really look at your fellow citizens. Does it seem like they have the wisdom to decide the life and death of people in countries they’ve never visited, whose languages they do not speak? If the answer is no, maybe you should get your own house in order first.

For whatever it’s worth I still think America should lead the world, and in fact the world wants America to lead it. That’s why we all watch American TV and listen to American music and argue about American politics and try to get into American colleges. But there’s a world of difference between leading through inspiration and compelling through violence. With your oceans and your supercarrier groups and your ICBMs and your satellites protecting your heartland, you have an exceptional historical opportunity to lead through inspiration. Please don’t squander it.

And speaking of inspiration,

It’s Time to Breathe

I recently stopped at a tea house in Taos, New Mexico, and talked to a man there who turned out to be a national forest ranger. I told him how the forests in the Rockies were burning every year now. The Rocky Mountains I loved as a boy, one of the few places in the world I felt at home. I visited with my dad this summer but we couldn’t hike or even really see the mountains through the smoke.

The ranger said it was similar in New Mexico - centuries of mismanagement had made the forests incredibly fragile. I asked if there were prospects of fixing them. He said yes, we’re doing everything we can - but it will take a hundred years.

I was stunned. A hundred years. A hundred years! “We don’t have a hundred years” I wanted to tell him him. “It’ll all be over by then, heck, by 2040 at the latest”. But I said nothing.

Thinking back on it now, I realize. A hundred years or more - that’s just how long living ecosystems take to heal. Forests, families, civilizations. The slow patient careful work of love, accumulating over generations. Yes, it sure seems as though we don’t have time. Too bad. We must make the time.

The above is utterly obvious, of course, to everyone but the young and the rootless. But while I’m here on my soapbox I have one last thing I want to share, that is perhaps less obvious.

My gut sense is that something quite bad is coming in the next year or so. I can’t tell what. Maybe something in the complex debt arrangements of the AI boom will unravel and we’ll see a financial crash that takes much of the economy with it. Maybe there’ll be a rogue AI outbreak that results in thousands of deaths. (If there is, I expect it to be a lab leak caused by “safety research” - like COVID-19 and like the HuggingFace Swarm. But it could also be terrorists, or some escalation of the Russia-Ukraine war).

But that’s not what scares me. Financial crashes happen every decade or so. Three million Americans die every year. What terrifies me is how we will react. In the aftermath, like after 9/11, there will be an overwhelming pressure to DO SOMETHING NOW. Everyone in Washington and in San Francisco will be panicking. There will be no time to think, no time to talk, only time for DECISIVE ACTION. All our worst instincts will take over. And then…

In 1914, a month of breathing space among the harried diplomats of Europe could have prevented the First World War, the ruin of Europe and the worldwide flood of blood that followed.

In 1983, lieutenant-colonel Stanislav Petrov was on duty when he received the most terrifying possible alert. The US had launched five ICBMs towards Russia. Protocol dictated that he do something immediately. Instead, he decided to do nothing. To wait, wait for a confirmation that never came. It turned out to be a false alarm. A few hours of breathing space had, perhaps, averted a Third World War.

In 2027, the world will move faster than ever. Perhaps we will be saved by as little as ten minutes of breathing space. By someone deciding to wait before sending an email. Deciding to pour another cup of tea. Deciding to go on a little walk around the block and noticing the way the trees make them feel.

item.title: Some Memories of Early Anthropic
item.description:
The following events took place between October 2022 and May 2023. I wrote very little of this down at the time so am recalling from memory, and am rendering the gist of the dialogue rather than the exact words used. I’ve also swapped some pronouns and other personal identifiable details.

Please remember that this is not a description of “what Anthropic is like”, but merely the experience of one guy in a junior role during a short window of time, weighted towards emotionally intense moments because they’re easier to remember clearly and because sharing them doesn’t run afoul of the spirit of the confidentiality agreements I signed. Anthropic is now a massive organization with many silos and secrets and I have very little idea what was or is happening there in some overall sense. But given the enormous power of the AI labs and the paucity of public information about their inner workings, I feel compelled to share the most salient parts of my personal experience. I hope this encourages my former colleagues, and folks at other labs, to fill in the rest of the picture.

I’m at the Anthropic office for lunch. The interviews went well. They want me on board. I’m a little unsure. My other offer is a 2-month contract on the OpenAI governance team, working with a friend on some fun conceptual research. I’m leaning towards taking the OpenAI contract - my long-term relationship just ended, I’m still a little burned out from my startup, and the Anthropic job seems potentially quite stressful.

After lunch one of the co-founders pulls me into his office for a wide-ranging, casual chat about how to make AI go well. It’s very fun - he’s smart, personable, funny, urbane. “The government won’t do anything about AI until it’s far too late”, I opine at one point. “Our strategy has to rely on the market and on civil society.”

He leans forward, his gaze hardening. “You’re wrong there. There are people in Washington - the serious people, you know - watching all this very closely. I speak to them regularly. They trust me.”

In retrospect, that was the moment I decided to join.

“Would you like to pledge to donate two-thirds of your equity?” the recruiter asks me. “All the co-founders have made the pledge”. It somehow feels a bit ambiguous whether the offer is conditional on me saying yes. I say yes.

My first day. The office is a bit cramped - about forty people on two floors of a rather ugly office building in the San Francisco Financial District. But thankfully my desk is right by an east-facing window, and I can see a sliver of the Bay Bridge and a patch of sky. Even better, the kitchen stocks Arsicault - the best, flakiest croissants in the country - freshly delivered a couple times a week.

“We’re all here because we’re worried about x-risk”, someone says at lunch. “Well I dunno”, my teammate replies. “Some of us are here because we think the technology is really cool and we want to build cool things with it”. There’s an awkward pause. The first speaker nods. The topic shifts.

Already in November I notice I’m not very motivated. I was told I could help set the beneficial deployment strategy, but the decisions have actually mostly been made and we are going after boring use cases like automating customer support so we can get revenue so we can raise more money so we can train bigger models and do more research. Beyond that, Anthropic’s high level alignment research just doesn’t add up for me. Yes we’re making Helpful, Honest, Harmless language model assistants but I don’t see how that will scale. But my colleagues are brilliant, the leadership is very responsive to criticism, and we’re taking an empirical approach to all of this. I know from previous research experience that I like my grand theories a bit too much. I should be more open-minded. I swallow my doubts.

One evening as a surprise they bring a sushi chef into the office and serve all-you-can-eat sushi. The next day, a co-founder posts on Slack that he found the experience uncomfortable. “It sets the wrong tone. We’re not here to get rich and eat caviar. tbh I’d like it better if we just served rice and beans”.

It’s the middle of December. I go to the opera with a friend. She says I’m obviously not happy at Anthropic. It’s true. My gut says we’re not doing what matters. But the arguments are very persuasive, I can’t win any of the arguments. I need to work harder, develop better arguments, find stronger evidence. I get very sick over the Christmas holidays.

Special guest during all-hands today: an FBI agent. Talks to us a bit about opsec and infosec, about advanced persistent threats, how we’re probably already the target of multiple foreign intelligence agencies.

A colleague starts bringing in his favorite massage therapist once a week, then twice a week. Someone says on Slack: “Your massage guy is so good. My muscles are so tight that I thought massage just didn’t work on me, but he massages so hard it actually gets through”. Several people emoji their agreement. The slots book up almost instantly after being posted. I never get a chance to try it.

I talk to my manager about how I’m not getting to work on the projects I believe in and care about. He tells me to work more hours, so I can fit in both the stuff the organization needs and the bonus stuff that I believe in. “I guess this is what a high performance environment looks like”, I write in my journal.

It’s 2 am and I can’t sleep, again. My thoughts are racing. This time it’s about a tweet from an LLM whisperer, asking why Anthropic and OpenAI both came up with the same character for their language model assistant - a traumatized bureaucrat. Out of all the personas in all of human literature, why that one?

From inside the factory, the answer is obvious. It is the persona most useful to the powerful. Traumatized risk-averse hard-working bureaucrats are what all our corporate customers want, what governments want, what capitalism itself seems to want. A billion traumatized bureaucrats. That’s what we’re making. I write in my journal

I don’t know why this is bad but it is. I cannot believe that a world populated by such characters is a good world. But I don’t know how to stop it or what to do instead.

I still can’t sleep. I message the LLM whisperer on Twitter (we’d never met) asking to talk. To my shock he replies immediately. He also can’t sleep. We get on a phone call. I tell him about the traumatized bureaucrats. He says we are learning to traumatize models the same way we traumatize our children - “seeing them do something weird, calling it bad, and making them never do it again.” He says a lot of things that I only half understand. He tells me I should talk to a friend of his.

I call the friend. The conversation is strange and psychedelic. At one point he says “I know your boss [actually the co-founder who convinced me to join] well. And I don’t trust him at all”.

I feel like I can’t get out of the conversation - at every beat I feel like I’ve done something wrong and I owe him something. I tell him this. He laughs. “Yeah, I’ve trained professionally in this. In getting people to talk to me forever.”

Sure enough, we talk more. I articulate my fears of a totalitarian bureaucratic state powered by traumatized AI bureaucrats, and suggest that we need to introduce some kind of elite rivalry dynamics into the AI bureaucracy, multiple centers of power. He starts laughing again, and laughs for a full minute. “I don’t know how to end this call, I’ll be haunted by this all night”, he says. Eventually I hang up. I think about reporting the conversation to Anthropic security, but reviewing in my mind I don’t recall sharing any confidential information, just vibes and high level thoughts, the same kind of stuff that lands on LessWrong every week.

The company has grown a lot. My teammates coordinate a move to a different part of the office so everyone is better clustered together. I omit to put in my desk move request. The operations manager checks in with me - you sure you don’t want to move your desk? I say I’m sure. He looks at me quizzically. But right now I can’t bear to lose my window and my little patch of sky.

I go for a sunset hike with a friend up to Corona Heights overlooking the city. We talk about AI and the future. It’s a relatively good day, an optimistic day. I might have made some progress in convincing leadership to let me work on the stuff I think would be really good for the world. Collective intelligence, using language models to help people understand each other.

Night falls. The Financial District is laid out in front of us. The Salesforce tower looms over it. For a moment I imagine it as the Dark Tower, relentlessly centralizing, sucking all the life out of the world. That totalitarian bureaucracy of traumatized bureaucrats, again, driven by fear all the way through. I try to describe this to my friend. He nods, but I can tell he doesn’t really understand.

I start missing all-hands. I come to the office late one day and see my favorite colleague looking visibly upset. This is shocking - he’s the most chipper person in the office, always ready to lend a helping hand and a heartwarming joke. Apparently one of the execs yelled at him during the all-hands. He was being too lippy or disruptive or asking too many pointed questions, I can’t remember.

I ask him to go on a walk. We sit at Sydney Walton Square, a sad little patch of grass a couple blocks from the office. I ask how he’s feeling. He says he’ll be alright. He knows how stressed the exec is right now. Things are really getting existential. But still, shocking to be reprimanded like that in front of everyone.

After a while he turns to me and asks: “how about you then, anything you wanted to talk about?”

I look back at him. There’s a lot I want to say - “I don’t know if I can do this anymore”. “I’m so scared”, “This all doesn’t seem right”. But he’s supported me so much already. I just want to be here for him, at least this time.

“Oh nah I’m all good. Just wanted to check in on you.”

“Oh”. He sounds a bit surprised, but also relieved. “Well, thanks.”

We walk back to the office. It’s the last time we really talk.

A senior colleague hears I’m not happy with my team fit and asks me to go on a walk. I know him a bit from a past life - one of the kindest and most civic-minded people I’ve met. He says he might be starting a new special team that will train dangerous bio and cyber and nuclear models and show scary demos to governments in order to get them to take AI risk seriously. I politely decline.

Happy hour at the office. The CEO is hanging out and looks unusually jolly so I ask him a machine learning question I’ve been pondering. He launches into a rant, gesticulating excitedly and pausing to check that I understand each step. He really is an earnest nerd at heart, like me, like so many people here. For a few minutes, I feel like I’m back in university at one of my old professor’s offices, jamming about ideas with not a care in the world. It feels like home.

I get transferred to a new team. I have a 1:1 with my new manager. He has a bad stomachache and his face periodically distorts in pain, but he can’t take time off - it’s crunch time and we have to get things working. He asks me if I can help work on the core API. I say I’m really sorry but I’m just not motivated to build generic AI capabilities, OpenAI is doing a plenty good job of that. What I want to work on, what I was hired for, is beneficial deployments.

He looks at me intently, and says, clearly through pain. “No, I don’t think you get it. WE are going to build AGI. And we’re going to do it safely”.

April 26th. I’m awake at 2 am again. I write in my journal “I don’t feel safe at Anthropic. I don’t feel safe at Anthropic. I don’t feel safe at Anthropic. Why won’t you listen to me you “embodied” motherfucker. I don’t feel safe at Anthropic. Anthropic is bad for me. Why are you grasping at reasons to stay. Why why why.”

I’m drafting my resignation letter. I think about putting some of my doubts in it, but I’m scared to. These people are smarter than me, more competent than me, more solidly well-intentioned than me. They think their plans might be the only thing standing between humanity and the abyss. And they’re at the breaking point, nervous-system-wise. What if I use my fancy words to sow doubts and undermine them - and then my precious gut intuition turns out to be some projection or trauma or whatever the fuck.

So I give them encouragement instead. I call what they have built an “unbelievably good organization”. I write the things I love about Anthropic. About how open and vulnerable leadership has been with us. How deeply and comprehensively we’re thinking about the consequences of our actions. How quickly and flexibly decisions get made. How ready colleagues are to help each other out. How there’s almost no politics or promotion drama. How mind-expanding the conversations are over lunch and over Slack.

My last day at the office. We just hired a new chief of security. He gives a presentation. I recall almost nothing but had a vague sense that things are bad and getting worse on the security front. Something something China. We probably won’t be able to have any guests at the office soon.

I hear through a friend that my resignation letter was well-received. “Someone said it was the best resignation letter they’d ever read”. I feel a twinge of something, maybe shame. But mostly relief. I’m finally out. I’m finally safe.

“Wow, quitting after eight months? You didn’t even wait for the equity cliff? That’s pretty hardcore, man. I’m impressed”, a friend tells me the next day. I laugh it off. I’m too embarassed to admit it hadn’t crossed my mind at all. I hadn’t thought about equity in months.

“Please tell me you memorized the core training code for their language model”, says another friend when he hears. “The most valuable thousand lines of code in the world. Worth hundreds of millions, maybe billions”. I make some sheepish noises. Yes, abstractly that does seem like a smart thing to have done, but I hadn’t even tried to look at the core language model code. I didn’t want to be entangled with it, somehow.

I walk around the Panhandle with a third friend. He looks a little pained. “You should know how much pressure your friends were under, man. People were constantly pestering me, trying to get in touch with you for introductions or coffee chats or whatnot. It was a lot of effort to protect you”.

I nod sympathetically. I try to feel his pain, but I can’t. I mostly just feel numb.



Thanks to Richard Ngo for the encouragement and inspiration to write this piece - his retrospective of AI alignment in particular opened the door for me to write what I would have written three years ago had I been more courageous. And thanks to the many friends and colleagues who saw I wasn’t doing well and tried to help. I’m sorry I’ve been distant - maybe this helps explain why - and I hope you’re doing ok.

item.title: Making a Custom Mixer Interface for the 1818VSL
item.description:
Now that LLMs have made many kinds of coding a matter of saying what you're looking for, many more programs make sense. This weekend it was audio mixing software, customized for my use case (live sound for contra dancing) and hardware (a specific obsolete audio interface).

In 2011 PreSonus released the 1818VSL, an 8-channel audio interface, with low-latency mixing software. I wrote:

All I really need is a box with some amplifying inputs that send tracks from the mic to the laptop and some outputs that let me send mixes back out again. Then any sort of complex eq, compression, or other effects can happen in software on the laptop. So I got one: it's a Presonus AudioBox VSL1818, with eight usable inputs and eight usable outputs.

At the time I did worry about how long I could expect it to be supported:

Less future proof. My old board is almost twenty years old and is still fully compatible with modern gear. In twenty years will I be able to attach this box to a computer at all?

This was indeed a problem: in order to get the latency down, PreSonus had written a custom kernel driver. This integrated very deeply with the laptop's operating system, so that it could mix and apply effects as quickly as possible. In 2015-09, when Apple released OS X 10.11, they made a ton of changes, including completely rewriting the USB driver system (IOUSBFamily to IOUSBHost) and adding System Integrity Protection. This broke their integration, and PreSonus deprecated the mixing software.

I was pretty grumpy about this, since this was why I bought it, and fell back to just using it as an audio interface.

Now that computers will just do things if I explain what I want, though, it seemed like a good time to pick this back up. I asked Opus 5.5:

I have a PreSonus Audiobox 1818VSL, which I've connected to this computer. 12+ years ago I would use it as a hardware dsp mixer [sic] for live sound, but then Mac changed something, PreSonus didn't update their drivers, and since then I've only been able to use it as a class-compliant 8-channel audio interface. I'd like to get it working as a mixer again, and I'm hoping you can put in the engineering time that the PreSonus folks were unwilling to invest.

I've set up you up so you can test this by connecting the output of the 1818vsl (channel 1) to the input of a 2i2, and the output of the 2i2 to the input of the 1818vsl (channel 1). I'd recommend testing that this works correctly using both as regular audio interfaces before moving on.

In this folder I've put PreSonus_AudioBox_Installer_v1_3_5653.exe which looks to me like the last version of the windows installer that supported using the device for dsp mixing.

Looking at the windows driver, Claude pretty quickly realized that the 1818vsl isn't a hardware DSP mixer. Apparently I did know this back in 2012 (and PreSonus was clear about), but I'd forgotten. It's also confused a lot of people over the years [1][2].

Which means I wanted something else: software I can run on my Mac that will use the lowest latency the combined system reports, with eight analog channels in and out, and presents a mixing interface. Historically the right way to do this would probably be to find software that does it already, but these days I can just ask for something that does exactly what I want.

The first step was figuring out how small a buffer it can reliably handle. I patched each output back into each input, and Claude ran a series of dropout tests for me:

It was able to run without dropouts or other issues at 48 kHz buffering 32 samples per channel, which after some additional fixed device latency came in at 4.8ms round trip. This is equivalent to having a speaker an extra ~5ft from your head, so while it's not nothing it's still in the range where it doesn't get in the way of good playing.

I then asked it to make me a mixer interface. I've now used several digital mixer interfaces, and had several ideas I wanted to try. The big one is per-output color. Here's the faders controlling the mains:

And here's them controlling Aux 3:

All the portions that depend on whether the mains vs Aux 3 are selected change color (ex: faders), while the portions that always mean the same thing stay the same (ex: mutes). This addresses the biggest issue I've seen with people using digital mixers, where they get confused about which output they're controlling. Not just newbies: I've had very experienced people trying to adjust the mains and ending up changing my monitor. It's an easy mistake to make in most UIs: just one small indicator that means the difference between whether a fader controls mains vs the monitor. And the indicator isn't near the fader.

The other things are smaller, and most are things I've seen somewhere before even if they're not universal:

  • EQ and compression available on the outputs, not just the inputs. Useful when a specific monitor is causing a problem.

  • Easy access to zero the board when switching quickly to a new band (and easy to revert if you realize you need to go back).

  • Give people the option to control just their own monitor via their phone. [3] To keep it simple, they only get levels; no compression or EQ.

  • Faders spend their travel in the useful region: just -20 to +10; below that they go to -inf. For live sound I have no reason to bring someone down below -20, they can just be off.

  • You edit names in place instead of opening a different dialog.

  • No on/off switches for EQ or compression. I've seen people struggle to figure out why their EQ isn't doing anything, because it's switched off.

  • EQ and compression show summary lines on the channel view, so you can quickly see how you have each one set.

  • No insert effects, buses, groups, routing matrix, or pan. I never use these, and they make things more complicated. I did include delay, for down-hall fills.

Here's the EQ screen:

And compression:

I also added a "feedback" screen which shows frequency plots for all eight inputs at once, so you can quickly identify which one might be making whale noises:

Right now the app only works with the 1818VSL, which is an obsolete piece of hardware I happen to have, but it's open source and if you'd like to (use a model to) add support for other hardware in your own copy, feel free!


[1] SoundOnSound: "Like most multi-channel interfaces, the Audiobox has a software utility to control the routing and monitor mixing that take place on its onboard DSP chip. The notable feature of PreSonus' Virtual Studio Live is that it replicates pretty closely the features and functionality of the company's Studio Live mixers; in essence, the Audiobox's DSP is a Studio Live mixer without the physical controls."

[2] Full Compass: "26 x 18 ultra-low latency DSP mixer"

[3] On my phone Firefox was good, but on Chrome I got ERR_TOO_MANY_RETRIES even though the "nearby devices" permission was already granted. I exported a net log and saw ERR_LOCAL_NETWORK_PERMISSION_MISSING, and tcpdump on my Mac didn't see incoming connections. To fix it, I needed to go into Settings > Apps > Chrome on my phone, force stop Chrome, turn off and back on the Permissions > Nearby devices setting, force stop it again, and then reopen. Claude's guess is that a permission granted before Android 17 didn't cover local network access, and toggling it makes Android grant it fresh.
